text:
Chapter Ten


Arthur was halfway to Atlantia on the two-lane highway that crisscrossed the marshlands when his phone dinged. He glanced down only for a moment, expecting an email, hoping for something from Maggie, but instead it was a calendar reminder: Lane’s appointment. Arthur cursed, turning on his signal and easing into the parking lot of a charging station before opening his phone and calling his brother, Rory.


It had been Rory who had persuaded him to go out on Beltane. “Live a little for once!” he’d shouted at him. “You’ve been working every day since you moved out here.” The party on Brig Beach was the same Beltane festival that Rory always bragged about when they were kids, calling Arthur at his mom’s to tell him about how he’d climbed out a window at their dad’s house and ridden his bike to the bonfire and all the requisite debauchery a teen boy could get into. Arthur had always been jealous of the stories, even if they were only half true. His mother would have eviscerated him for sneaking out, so he’d never tried it, not even when he was with his dad over the summer in Atlantia, convinced she would find out somehow.


But when Rory suggested they go to that same festival a few weeks ago, Arthur had felt seventeen again. All that envy and regret and excitement bubbled up until he said yes. In fact, Arthur had revealed all of that to Rory after about five minutes of wearing that damn mask. He’d confessed all of his childhood envies, the way he’d thought to relive some of the nights he’d missed out on now, at thirty-five. It had been a ridiculous thing to say, and Rory hadn’t let him forget it, not that night and not since. Rory had resurrected old insults the way only a brother can, so Arthur had abandoned Rory on Beltane, afraid of what else he’d reveal.


Arthur had been too distracted in the weeks since. His baby brother needed him, and he couldn’t believe he’d forgotten about Lane’s appointment. He felt like a bad brother and a worse uncle. He cursed again as the phone rang.


“Hey, Artie.” Rory’s voice came through the line after a few more rings. He sounded far away, and the screeching of kids echoed in the background. Before Arthur could answer, Rory’s voice was muffled as he yelled, “I know you’re not making a pet out of that poisonous caterpillar right now.” Arthur waited a moment for Rory to come back to him. “Yeah, well, I’m not Geordie’s dad,” he went on, still muffled, and then his voice was clear through the receiver again. “Sorry,” he finally said, exasperated. “This kid is out of control.”


Arthur knew he didn’t mean it.


“He’s had a very long day, studying hard,” Arthur said, defending his only nephew, who was perfect in every way.


“I know, I know.”


“You still at the school?”


“I’m letting him burn off some energy at the playground. Kid’s made a friend with a fourth grader and is causing havoc.” Rory sighed, and Arthur could imagine him sitting on the top of one of the warped, weather-beaten picnic tables that surrounded the school playground, his worry plain on his face.


“Steph couldn’t pick him up today?” Arthur didn’t mean to sound accusatory. Rory and his ex-wife had a good relationship, but he sometimes felt a fiery overprotectiveness for his brother and nephew that he had a hard time stifling. Rory and Stephanie had married young, barely out of college, while Arthur was still in the worst part of his PhD. It had been one of those times when Arthur had felt every mile between him and his brother. Steph and Rory’s marriage had already started to fall apart when she got pregnant, but Arthur hadn’t even known they were having problems. He sometimes wondered whether he could have made that hard time easier for Rory. If he had been a better brother. If he’d been here.


“She’s out of town on a business trip, but she’s already called about five times to check in. Besides”—Rory sighed—“I’d rather be worrying about Simon on the monkey bars than, well, you know.”


Arthur opened his mouth to say something but then hesitated. Rory must have been able to tell through the phone, because he answered Arthur’s unspoken question about Lane before he could ask it. “I haven’t heard from Pop or my mom yet.”


Arthur’s stomach dipped. Lane’s appointment had been scheduled for hours before, and Arthur had no idea if the delay meant anything, good or bad. He should be the one with experience here, but he felt like he was floundering.


“I’m on my way back to Atlantia. I’ll stop at Angelo’s and pick up a pizza,” he offered, trying to feel useful.


Rory’s relief was palpable through the phone. “That’s great. Can you get my mom an order of the fried ravioli? She loves those.”


“Of course. Give Simon a hug for me.”


After Rory hung up, Arthur pulled back out onto the highway toward Atlantia, which had finally come into view, rising out of the lowland marshes like a beacon. As he drove, his stomach tied itself into tighter and tighter knots.


Rory was, technically, Arthur’s half brother, but they’d never made that distinction. Rowena and Barry, Arthur’s parents, had a short-lived marriage that ended before Arthur was born. He grew up primarily with his mother, other than the long summer weeks at his father’s bungalow in North Atlantia. Barry’s second marriage to Lane, Rory’s mom, had ended, too, but Barry and Lane had stayed good friends, unlike the tense animosity that lasted between Rowena and Barry until right before Rowena passed away. Even though Barry wasn’t married to Lane anymore, it was clear they still loved each other deeply. They just loved each other from separate houses.


After his mother died, Arthur had been lost. His whole life had been spent orbiting Rowena. He had inherited her dark hair, her same aspirations, an academic career built on the research she’d explained to him instead of reading bedtime stories. She had been a larger-than-life presence. When she was gone and her own legacy hadn’t been enough to save her from a terrible end, he wondered what it had all been for. Did he even want the life he’d been building for almost twenty years? Or had Rowena wanted it? He didn’t know. After finishing out that year teaching at Dartwood, the only thing he knew for sure was that he couldn’t live across the country from the only family he had left.


So, he’d reached out to Dean Bobbin and had a job at Hawthorn within a week. Despite his misgivings about the job, he loved being in Atlantia with his dad, Rory, and Simon. And when Lane’s health scare had frightened them all, a near replay of what had happened with Rowena, he knew he’d made the right decision. This was why he’d moved here—to be here for his father and brother when they needed him.


The bungalow was still dark when he arrived, greasy pizza and fried ravioli in hand, but he didn’t let himself think about what that might mean. He set the boxes of food on the table, but before he could put the rest of his stuff down, his phone buzzed.




Magnolia Linden, PhD: It’s been 97 minutes, Taliesin. Are you alive?




He smiled to himself as he looked down at the screen and shrugged off his bag, heavy with books he’d brought home from the library, and added his shoes to the pile by the front door. Another message came in.




Magnolia Linden, PhD: Send proof of life






Arthur: I’m alive






Magnolia Linden, PhD: Flimsy proof. How do I know you’re not texting from beyond the veil, doomed to haunt the labs of Ilex Hall forever?




He snorted, though if he let himself think about death for too long, he felt a familiar bubbling anxiety. He pushed it down, like he always did, and went to snap a picture of himself, but he was horrified when he opened the camera on his phone. The dark circles under his eyes looked like deep bruises, and the grays in his stubble were too obvious for his liking. Instead, he flipped the camera around and took a picture of his hand against the window. His truck was in the background, surrounded by scraggly scrub grass. Before he could send it off, another text came in.




Magnolia Linden, PhD: RIP




His grin grew again as he sent off the photo he’d taken.




Arthur: Not a ghost (yet)






Magnolia Linden, PhD: Thank goodness




It was probably pathetic to read into that “thank goodness,” but Arthur did it anyway.


“What are you smiling at?” came Rory’s voice, muffled through the storm door. He was followed closely on his heels by Simon.


“Uncle Artie! Uncle Artie!” Simon chanted as he sprinted inside. Arthur carefully slid his phone into his pocket before swooping Simon up into his arms.


“Who wouldn’t smile with such a cute nephew around?” Rory narrowed his eyes but didn’t press. Arthur knew he had other things on his mind.


Simon rambled about something that had happened on the playground and Arthur nodded along, as distracted as Rory. He wandered back into the kitchen with Simon, Rory right behind them, and deposited his nephew at the kitchen sink to wash his hands.


Rory leaned over his son to help him. They looked like twins, just separated by a few decades, with their matching curly brown hair, a shade lighter than Arthur’s, the same freckled skin, the same quirked half smiles when they told jokes. Simon looked so much like the little boy Arthur still thought of first before remembering Rory was grown.


As Arthur arranged plates on the table around the pizza box, Rory scrubbed playground dirt from beneath Simon’s fingernails. “Uncle Artie, are you coming to my baseball game?”


Arthur didn’t care if he had to rearrange his entire schedule, he’d already planned to be at every game. “Of course.”


Rory helped Simon down from the sink, and the boy dashed off to his room. “He sits on the bench for most of the game and reads, but he loves it,” Rory grumbled, but there was a note of pride in his voice as he added, “Reminds me of his uncle.”


Arthur watched his brother, looking for signs of worry on his face, but Rory was consumed by making sure Simon was settled for dinner. He put a slice of pizza on a plate for him and poured him a glass of lemonade, grabbing napkins and forks and knives. Finally, when there was nothing left that anyone could conceivably need for a pizza dinner, Rory sat down. Simon was happily eating, but Rory kept watching the clock, nervously biting the skin at his nail.


“Hey, whatever happens,” Arthur said, “we’ll figure it out. I’ll call in favors, we’ll get her the best…” Rory nodded his head toward Simon, who had stopped eating his pizza to look at the two men. Arthur finished his sentence with, “Ice cream.”


Simon perked up at that. “Ice cream?” he repeated, a gleam in his eyes. Rory gave Arthur an exasperated look and Arthur shrugged.


“Uncle privilege! We’ll go out for ice cream later.” He ruffled Simon’s hair until the boy grimaced into his pizza.


When the storm door swung open, slamming against the wall of the bungalow like it had for Arthur’s entire life, Rory shot up. “We’re home,” Barry called, followed by the familiar sounds of his arrival. He dropped his keys into a metal dish with a clang, and after muffled badgering from Lane, they heard him slide open the coat closet door to drop off his shoes.


“You don’t live here anymore, Laney,” Barry muttered, his tone exasperated, but Arthur noted his father’s affectionate name for his ex-wife.


“Thank the gods above for that,” Lane retorted.


Rory gave Simon a nervous glance, but Arthur gestured to the front of the house with his head. “Go,” he mouthed. Rory nodded his thanks and left the kitchen.


Their conversation was muted, and Arthur couldn’t make out the words. He kept an eye on Simon, who had finished his pizza and was now distracted by the Captain Long Johns book he was flipping through. Arthur tapped his foot, his own anxiety climbing higher.


This November would mark two years since Rowena Taliesin’s death. Arthur couldn’t believe how time continued to march on without her in it. It just didn’t make sense. Her brief illness had been brutal, but Rory had been there for him as much as he could be, and Arthur was relieved that, if his brother needed him in the same way, he could be here for him.


Suddenly there was a burst of laughter from the living room and Rory returned, a relieved grin on his face. “Everything’s fine,” he said, and Arthur sagged against his chair. “The test came back negative.”


“I told all of you to stop worrying about me,” Lane said as she came into the kitchen. “Just because I’m getting old doesn’t mean you stop listening to your mother and gramma,” she chastised gently, kissing Simon on top of his head. She gave Arthur’s shoulder a squeeze, too.


He reached up and patted her hand, leaning into her touch. “I’m so happy to hear the good news.”


Rory herded his mother into one of the seats at the table and disappeared to find her something to drink. “Stop fussing, Rory,” she insisted.


“Listen to your mother,” came Barry’s gruff command. He took the seat next to Lane, pulling a still-steaming slice of pizza onto his plate.


“I refuse,” Rory responded, beaming at his mother. As the tension melted from the room, everyone’s expressions infused with that unique joy that can only come when the worst has been dodged. As they talked and ate, laughter filling the tiny kitchen, Arthur suddenly felt like time had folded in on itself and he was fourteen to Rory’s twelve, a sometimes interloper in this family unit that, for better or worse, was stuck with him for most of the summer.


Lane yawned and Rory stood, clearing her plate from in front of her before she could get to it. “I’m driving Mom home,” he announced.


“Don’t be ridiculous,” she argued. “It’s down the block, and I’m perfectly capable of walking.”


“You don’t be ridiculous,” he answered. “I’m driving you home.” She rolled her eyes but smiled despite herself. Lane planted a kiss on Barry’s balding head, whispering something in his father’s ear that Arthur couldn’t quite make out, and then followed Rory out of the kitchen.


“Simon, I’m taking Gramma back to her house,” Rory called out. “Watch your uncle for me.” Simon nodded solemnly, as if Arthur needed a lot of supervision, which, gods below, he probably did.



—


Arthur made good on his promise to get Simon ice cream, sending the boy home with his dad on a sugar high later that evening. They would be back early in the morning so Barry could take Simon fishing, and Arthur decided he would tell Rory about Beltane and Maggie then. Maybe. He’d sleep on it.


Arthur left his dad to snore in his reclining chair with the weather radio station on in the background, returning to the same childhood bedroom he’d always had at his dad’s house. Though he only used it over the summer, Barry had kept it set up for Arthur how he’d liked it as a kid, and it looked much the same now as it did then. There was a small twin bed that Arthur was much too tall for. On the walls, there were posters, pictures cut out from newspapers and magazines, and photos. The themes shifted from the trains he’d been obsessed with as a young boy to book and album covers to a Dartwood pennant he’d hung the summer he applied to colleges, as well as photos of him and Rory at twelve, fifteen, and twenty. He’d recently added one of him holding a tiny Simon and another that they took after one of Simon’s baseball games last summer. Above a desk he’d never fit in now, there was a corkboard full of pretend runes and fake spells he’d invented as a kid. His dad had saved them and pinned them on the board for “inspiration” when Arthur moved back in. And then, in the corner of the corkboard, was the mask from that night, the blooms starting to curl at the edges as they dried.


He flopped on the bed, idly opening his phone and pulling up the text exchange with Maggie. He typed out a message and then stared at it, trying to gather enough courage to send it. In one motion, he hit send and then tossed the phone across his bed like it was on fire.




Arthur: What are you doing Thursday after classes end?




When she didn’t answer right away, Arthur’s stomach dropped. It was obviously too late to be texting a colleague. He shouldn’t have done it. Is it weird to text her at all? he thought, forgetting that she had been the one to message him first. He was about to throw his phone into the sea and pretend it never happened, when she responded.




Magnolia Linden, PhD: Ideally, I will be horizontal. Bed. Couch. I’m not a picky woman.




Arthur nearly choked. His skin flushed hot, realizing what she meant, but even imagining Maggie curled up on the couch after a long day of teaching, wearing a pair of skintight leggings, hair piled in a bun, was enough. He tried, unsuccessfully, to banish the image from his mind.




Arthur: What if, instead, we went to Bean There, Done That?




Gods, that coffee shop had such a ridiculous name. He couldn’t believe someone had put that on a business license. It was as if these small-town shops had one marketing plan and it was a pun.


He looked back at the text and realized he didn’t say anything about why he was asking her to get coffee. He quickly typed out:




Arthur: I’ll bring all my research. My last class ends at 4.






Magnolia Linden, PhD: Only if you buy me one of their cream cheese pastries.






Arthur: It’s the least I could do.






Magnolia Linden, PhD: I’ll meet you there at 5.




Thursday. He had almost a week to figure out what, exactly, he was going to tell Maggie about their shared night on Brig Beach, about the pall. His mouth was suddenly dry. He was sure Maggie would be incandescent with rage when she found out he was the man she’d kissed and that he’d kept it from her. It would be all over. They obviously wouldn’t be able to share an office. Shouldn’t work together at all. He just wanted a few more days before she was out of his life forever. Before all the color that had come back to him would be banished back to gray.


He was about to hit the power button so he could stop thinking about text messages and the pall and just sleep, when Maggie’s name popped up again: Good night, Taliesin.

facts.fact: 高速上日历提醒 Lane 的预约——他忘了；愧疚致电 Rory。
Beltane 是 Rory 劝的（Live a little）；真话符文下五分钟他招尽童年妒羡，Rory 至今取笑。
家族谱系：Rory 是同父异母（Barry×Lane）；Barry 与 Lane 离婚后仍至交，与 Rowena×Barry 的一世交恶相反。
facts.anchor: Rory was, technically, Arthur’s half brother

facts.fact: 母亲 Rowena 之死：他一生环绕她运转——黑发、志向、讲解研究而非读睡前故事。
facts.anchor: His whole life had been spent orbiting Rowena

facts.fact: 存在之问：二十年的人生是谁想要的？辞 Dartwood 一周内拿到 Hawthorn 职，为守 Atlantia 家人。
短信战：她 97 分钟计时催平安、要存活证明、发 RIP；他回手掌照 Not a ghost (yet)。
Simon 与 Rory 像隔了几十年的双胞胎；uncle privilege 冰激凌之约。
facts.anchor: They looked like twins, just separated by a few decades

facts.fact: Lane 检查阴性——全家如释重负；那是 Rowena 剧本的 near replay。
深夜邀约：周四 Bean There, Done That 带全部研究资料；他怕摊牌后颜色重回灰。
